newsitem.title: PERU: Shell plans first well at Peru's Camisea in February.
newsitem.headline: Shell plans first well at Peru's Camisea in February.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell plans to drill three exploratory wells starting next February to appraise the reserves in Peru's huge Camisea oil condensate and gas fields, a company official said Monday.

The first well will be drilled in the Cashiriari field, where data will be collected for 100 days before the company moves on to drill wells in the San Martin field and a second in Cashiriari, Shell Prospecting and Development (Peru) B.V. spokesman Andrew Vickers said in an interview.

These two fields and the smaller Mipaya make up the Camisea reserves, situated 310 miles (500 km) east of Lima and estimated to hold 11 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and 600 million barrels of natural gas liquids.
Shell was also considering using the one well that has previously been drilled in Camisea area - at the Cashiriari field - for production of gas as early as 1999, Vickers said.
The full development project should bring gas to Lima around 2002, he added.
Oil giants Shell and Mobil signed a contract with the government in May that gives them the rights for two years to appraise Camisea's reserves with a view to developing them.
Shell estimates it will invest over $100 million in this two-year period, Vickers said.
In late August, Peruvian authorities formally approved the company's assessment of the project's impact on the environment and local indigenous communities, Vickers said.
This allowed Shell to start immediately building a base camp at Nuevo Mundo in the Camisea area, from which the company transports equipment to the fields by hovercraft, he added.

If the oil consortium, in which Shell is the operating partner with a 57.5 percent share, exploits the reserves, the project will last 40 years and become the largest foreign investent commitment in Peru at an estimated $2.6 billion.
The fields hold six times the rest of the country's reserves, according to the government, which estimates it will receive $6 billion in tax revenue from the project during the first 30 years.
The oil consortium envisages building a pipeline to transport the Camisea gas for sale in Lima, where Shell is working to establish a market amongst industrial companies, Vickers said.
The project also considers the option of supplying gas to fuel a new 600 megawatt (MW) power plant expected before 2000 ahead of the main development of the fields.
Shell and Mobil have selected a U.S. consortim of International Generating Company (Intergen) and Community Energy Alternatives (CEA) to negotiate exclusively a gas sale and purchase contract.
Shell and Mobil would use early production from the Cashiriari well to supply gas to the proposed power plant, Vickers said.
The electricity consortium is evaluating the plant's construction to supply 300 MW to Lima and 300 MW for the south of the county, in part to serve the needs of mining companies.
Shell and Mobil have also been negotiating with the government since June over rights to explore an area, block 75, to the west and northwest of Camisea.
